Can you provide examples of baseball players whose Hall of Fame careers were negatively affected by poor ballparks? These are are Hall of Fame baseball players whose careers were negatively affected by their home ballparks: Joe DiMaggio hit only 41% of his home runs at home. As great as he was, Joltin’ Joe may have been far greater at a friendlier hitting park for right-handed power hitters. Yankee Stadium from 1923 to 1973 was a graveyard for right-handed sluggers, with a left-center power alley up to a mammoth 457 feet deep. As a result, DiMaggio had a 1.016 OPS on the road, and .938 at home, for a difference of -.78. That 1.016 OPS would be sixth all-time among MLB players, and better than Rogers Hornsby, Aaron Judge, Mike Trout, Mickey Mantle and Stan Musial. A good example of the problem DiMaggio faced is his teammate Gil McDougald, who hit only 26% of his home runs at home. McDougald had a 121 tOPS+ on the road, but just 78 at home. Also, Elston Howard, who joined the Yankees shortly after DiMaggio’s retirement and hit only 32% of his home runs at home. Stan Musial was nominated in the comments by Gil Johnson with the following observation: “I would add Stan Musial to that list. He played in cavernous St. Louis ballparks, which reduced the number of home runs he hit—but increased the number of triples. He never led the league in homers, but topped the NL in triples five times.” Goose Goslin hit only 37% of his home runs at home. Other Washington Senators stars like Mickey Vernon and Eddie Yost had even lower home homer rates. Why? Griffith Stadium was arguably the worst home run park of all time. Mike Piazza may have had even better hitting stats if he didn’t play half his games at Dodger Stadium. Andre Dawson played in Montreal during his prime. Le Stade Olympique was built for the 1976 Olympics and has been called the worst MLB ballpark of all time. Once Dawson moved to Chicago his hitting stats skyrocketed. Rusty Staub might be in Hall of Fame if he hadn’t played in the Houston Astrodome during its “deadball era” between 1964 and 1969. That was the hardest time to hit in the history of the toughest park to hit in. Cesar Cedeno and Jim Wynn were also greatly disadvantaged by the cavernous Astrodome dimensions. Conversely, these are the ten HOF players who benefited most from their home ballparks, with the largest career difference in OPS between their home and away splits: Bobby Doerr +.214 Chuck Klein +.214 Hank Greenberg +.210 Larry Walker +.203 Todd Helton +.193 Earl Averill +.163 Ron Santo +.158 Roy Campanella +.157 Wade Boggs +.153 Jimmie Foxx +.150 … Ralph Kiner +.124 Mel Ott +.062 (discussed below) Mickey Mantle +.039 Babe Ruth +0.33 Willie Mays +.022 Hank Aaron +.014 (and just 15 more homers at home) Lou Gehrig -.047 Joe DiMaggio -.078 (just think of Joltin’ Joe in a friendlier home park for righties!) Home ballparks can and do make a difference in Hall of Fame careers. But in some cases, like Joe DiMaggio’s, especially, the results can be a downer. Mel Ott’s name came up in the comments, as expected. This is my analysis: Mel Ott hit more home runs at the Polo Grounds with that short porch, but he hit a lot more doubles and triples on the road and ended up with nearly the same total bases: 2552 at home, 2488 away. And he hit .311 on the road versus .297 at home. Ott’s .062 OPS differential is less than half that of the top ten. And his .918 road OPS ties him with Albert Pujols’ career mark and is better than than the career marks of Mike Schmidt, Dick Allen, Miguel Cabrera, Willie McCovey, Willie Stargell and Harmon Killebrew. by Michael R. Burch

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? THE CASE FOR JESUS MYTHICISM by Michael R. Burch Is there a case for Jesus mythicism — the idea that Jesus of Nazareth was entirely a myth, not a real person? Before I explore the issue, let me say that I think — not “believe” or “know,” but more of an educated guess — that there probably was an obscure Jewish rabbi that no one in power knew or cared anything about. Thus no trial before Pilate or Herod. No miracles except maybe a faith healing here and there. No walking on water, which is physically impossible. No claiming to be “god” or the “unique son of god” which would have gotten Jesus stoned to death, probably. And probably no crucifixion, since the cross was not mentioned in regard to Christianity outside the shamelessly fudged New Testament texts, until the second century AD, from what I understand. But possibly an empty grave and wild rumors of a “resurrection” that inspired the religion we now call Christianity. However, it bears noting that if there was an empty grave, the case for a “real” resurrection falls apart because it’s clear from the four gospels and the book of Acts that no one had a clue what happened to Jesus after the alleged “resurrection.” A resurrection without a resurrectee is not very impressive! Think about it. If you interacted with the resurrected God who had died for the sins of the world and was offering you salvation and the gift of eternal life in heaven, wouldn’t you remember where you saw him and what he said and did? But no one in the New Testament had a clue, so five different accounts all say radically different things. True believers do not make up sh-t about the God they truly believe in. Only charlatans trying to manipulate other people would that. However, it is possible that there was a real Jesus and rumors of an empty grave, explaining the core belief, and that the outrageous lying came later, as the cult expanded and charlatans began manipulating it for their own purposes. But again, this is just what I think, and I believe there is a very good case for Jesus mythicism. Here’s why… First, there is not a shred of testimony by any contemporary of Jesus, outside the Bible, that he actually lived. Josephus was born after the alleged death of Jesus and thus could not have been an eyewitness. Furthermore, the tiny bits Josephus allegedly “wrote” about Jesus were clearly either added entirely or heavily forged by Christian charlatans. We know this because if a religious Jew like Josephus had really believed Jesus was the Messiah, he would have written a LOT more about the most important figure, not only in Jewish history, but in the history of the world. If you were writing the history of Christianity, would you give Jesus three rushed sentences, then write a massive tome about far lesser figures like Andrew and Thomas? Of course not, and neither would Josephus dash off three sentences about someone he believed to be the Messiah. Here is what Josephus allegedly wrote: “Now, there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man, for he was a doer of wonderful works—a teacher of such men as receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews, and many of the Gentiles. He was [the] Christ; and when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men amongst us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him, for he appeared to them alive again the third day, as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him; and the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day.” The forgers were apparently cramped for space. They had no knowledge of Israel at the time of Jesus, saying he drew the Gentiles when Jesus said himself that he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel and it was Paul who drew Gentiles to Christianity after Jesus’s death. Also the Jews have no belief that the Messiah will die and be resurrected, so Josephus would not have said that. Nor do the Jews believe the prophets foretold “ten thousand wonderful things” about the Messiah. The entire passage is what Christians believe about Jesus, not what first century Jews believed about the Messiah. And “not extinct to this day” sounds like someone writing in the 2nd or 3rd century AD, after Roman attempts to get rid of Christians had failed, not something someone would write a few years after Jesus’s death. The Testimonium Flavianum is clearly the work of forgers. Does an all-powerful God need forgers to “help” him make himself known to human beings? It seems unlikely to me. Second, there is also not a shred of testimony by any eyewitness inside the Bible, that Jesus existed. We have no testimony from any of the apostles, which seems very, very odd. We don’t hear any NT author saying “Peter told me this” or “James told me that.” The apostles other than Judas all survived Jesus, and any true believer would have moved heaven and earth to get their testimonies, but we have none. Nada. Nil. Very, very odd indeed. Third, it’s beyond obvious that large parts of Jesus’s “life” were lifted directly from myths of far more ancient “saviors” like Dionysus, Horus, Krishna, Mithra, Romulus, et al. “Anything your savior can do, mine can do better!” seems to have been the modus operandi of the authors and redactors of the New Testament. Clearly mythical features of the “life” of Jesus that were plagiarized from more ancient “saviors” include: This is “been there, done that” for any number of ancient saviors. No right-thinking person can believe such copycatted nonsense, so the question becomes: Was there a real Jesus whose “resume” got padded by really bad liars who couldn’t keep their lies straight, or was Jesus always entirely mythical? While I believe there is a strong case for Jesus mythicism, I lean toward a real, entirely human and nonmagical Jesus, for primarily one reason: Mary Magdalene The only consistent thing about the entire New Testament — a book full of wild lies and wilder contradictions — is that Mary Magdalene was at the empty grave and that whatever role she played made her impossible to write out. The fact that none of the lying male chauvinist authors of the Bible were able to write out Mary Magdalene in favor of penis-equipped Peter or John makes me think it was widely known that she was the first Christian. And the most likely reason for that is that something made Mary Magdalene think Jesus was alive despite his having died. It could have been an empty grave. It could have been some sort of dream or vision. There could have been some sort of near death experience (NDE). Such things are not uncommon. I am not a Christian, but an agnostic. I don’t believe Jesus walked on water, turned water into wine, or raised the dead. I don’t think he was resurrected bodily and was walking through walls, soaring into the clouds like Superman, etc. But it’s not that unusual for people to think they have seen and/or communicated with their departed loved ones. My educated guess is that something happened that made Mary Magdalene think Jesus was still alive, even though no one else ever saw or spoke to him, requiring the authors of the four gospels and Acts to make up five incompatible lie-filled stories about what happened after the “resurrection.” It’s too bad we don’t have Mary Magdalene’s account of what happened. Maybe one day it will turn up. If so, I suspect the Christian world will be shocked from its crown to its toes. by Michael R. Burch

Do you think in the future Oleksandr Usyk will share the title of the greatest fighter of all time with Muhammad Ali? First, we must recognize that Muhammad Ali is just one of three main contenders to be boxing’s GOAT. In most pound-for-pound rankings the order is: In my opinion Oleksandr Usyk is not in this exalted company for the following reasons: Usyk has not faced the kind of competition the BIG THREE faced. As the saying goes, “To be the MAN you have to beat the MAN.” But Usyk has not faced and defeated an all-time great boxer, so his resume is lacking and time is running out, without a great boxer on the horizon with whom to prove his mettle. Usyk had a late start as a professional boxer, at age 26, and thus his 22-0 record with just 14 knockouts at age 37 is decidedly light for a GOAT candidate. Usyk has had only ten heavyweight fights, four of those as a cruiserweight. So Usyk has only fought as a true heavyweight six times. Matt McGrain ranks Usyk #19 at heavyweight, which is strong for his limited number of fights, but far from GOAT territory. 18 – Ezzard Charles 19 – Oleksandr Usyk 20 – Jersey Joe Walcott Usyk is also the WBN #19 heavyweight. But I think that’s too high. Here’s why. I rank the following heavyweights above Usyk, whom I have at #24. I have Norton ranked above most of the boxing experts. At one point in his career he was 41-5 with four of those losses to all-time greats: Ali, Foreman and Holmes. Norton would probably have been 44-1 in any other era. Is Ken Norton the most underrated heavyweight of all time? That well may be. I can see him as high as #11 in my ranking of the all-time heavyweights. Norton had wins over Ali, Jimmy Young, Jerry Quarry, Randall “Tex” Cobb and Duane Bobick. The ultimate compliment to Norton came from his rival Muhammad Ali: “I decided to regain my title (after losing it to Leon Spinks) and then retire because I knew I didn't have another Norton fight in me." Larry Holmes, who fought Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield in their primes, agreed with Ali, saying: “My toughest and best opponent was Ken Norton, no doubt.” Holmes also said: “After Norton, all my other title defenses were pieces of cake. He was tough, he was strong, he was hard to hit!" Yes, I think the great Ken Norton has been underrated. (#19) Jersey Joe Walcott (49-20-1) is the #14 heavyweight per Bill Caplan, #15 per SportsRatings, #16 per Brian Wilbur, #17 per IBRO, #17 per GiveMeSport, #19 per Monte Cox, #20 per Boxing-dot-com, #20 per Boxing Action, Fight City top 30, and #24 per Ranker. He’s the #43 boxer per Ranker and #79 per BoxRec. I believe Walcott has been underrated due to early and late losses. But there are extenuating circumstances because his father died when he was 15 and he had to work to support his mother and 11 younger siblings. That left little time to train and no money for training camps. Walcott often took fights on short notice because he needed the money and had little or no time to prepare for such fights with his other obligations. Due to such factors he was a late bloomer, but he went on an 18-3 run in which two of his losses were to all-time greats Elmer Ray and Joey Maxim, and he came back to avenge both losses, beating Ray once and Maxim twice. By the time Walcott faced Joe Louis for the heavyweight championship in 1947, he may have been the best heavyweight on the planet. Walcott also clearly outboxed Rocky Marciano in their first fight but got caught by a devastating haymaker in the 13th round that he couldn’t get up from. But at the height of his powers Jersey Joe could box with anyone, and outfox anyone in the ring. He was a defensive warlock with power in both hands. He may have been the most skilled heavyweight of all time, or second only to Ali. Walcott had signature wins over Ezzard Charles (twice), Joey Maxim (twice), Elmer Ray, and Joe Louis (in the opinion of many). What is the most difficult book to write? A collection of short stories, a collection of poems or a novel? Any book is easy to write. To write a really good book is an entirely different matter. Between a collection of short stories, a collection of poems, and a novel, I rank the difficulty as follows: 3. I think a collection of short stories would be the easiest to write because short stories are generally less complex than novels and usually have a narrower focus, less historical information and buildup, etc. In a short story there is usually less to manage than in a novel, and thus less to get out of the writer’s control. A long novel like War and Peace has to remain consistent and coherent from start to finish. A change toward the end may require multiple adjustments earlier in the book. And so on. And think of the complexity of a series of novels like The Lord of the Rings trilogy. The mind boggles. 2. I think a novel is easier to write than an outstanding collection of poems because writing evocative poetry lies beyond the ability of most writers. For example, Mark Twain was a great novelist and writer of short stories, but at best a competent poet. 1. Anyone can write a poem, but few writers can manage really good poetry, much less great poetry. How many of the great novelists have written a single great poem? On the other hand, great poets have written the equivalents of novels, short stories and/or plays, and of an exceedingly high order: The ancient Sumerian poem The Epic of Gilgamesh reads like a novel. Homer’s Odyssey and Iliad read like novels. Virgil’s Aeneid reads like a novel. Dante’s epic Divine Comedy reads like a novel. The ancient Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf reads like a novel. Geoffrey Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales reads like a collection of short stories. Christopher Marlowe’s verse plays read like novels or novellas. Edmund Spenser’s Faerie Queene reads like a fantasy novel. William Shakespeare’s verse plays read like novels or novellas. John Milton’s Paradise Lost reads like a novel. Walt Whitman’s poems in Leaves of Grass read like a collection of flash fiction. Oscar Wilde wrote plays and the novella The Picture of Dorian Gray. and so on… Some of the greatest stories ever told, were told with the additional complexities of poetry tossed in. There have been great short stories and novels, but the writers were scaling the Ozarks while Homer, Virgil, Dante, Chaucer, Shakespeare and Milton assaulted the Himalayas. by Michael R. Burch

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? WHAT BECAME OF HELEN OF TROY? by Michael R. Burch The truth is that we really don’t know what happened to Helen of Troy after the fabled city fell, because there are various conflicting accounts. In “To Have Loved” rather than making up something, I imagine Helen like so many women in times of war, embracing her husband while wondering what will become of her when he dies… To Have Loved by Michael R. Burch "The face that launched a thousand ships ..." Helen, bright accompaniment, accouterment of war as sure as all the polished swords of princes groomed to lie in mausoleums all eternity ... The price of love is not so high as never to have loved once in the dark beyond foreseeing. Now, as dawn gleams pale upon small wind-fanned waves, amid white sails, ... now all that war entails becomes as small, as though receding. Paris in your arms was never yours, nor were you his at all. And should gods call in numberless strange voices, should you hear, still what would be the difference? Men must die to be remembered. Fame, the shrillest cry, leaves all the world dismembered. Hold him, lie, tell many pleasant tales of lips and thighs; enthrall him with your sweetness, till the pall and ash lie cold upon him. Is this all? You saw fear in his eyes, and now they dim with fear’s remembrance. Love, the fiercest cry, becomes gasped sighs in his once-gallant hymn of dreamed “salvation.” Still, you do not care because you have this moment, and no man can touch you as he can ... and when he’s gone there will be other men to look upon your beauty, and have done. Smile—woebegone, pale, haggard. Will the tales paint this—your final portrait? Can the stars find any strange alignments, Zodiacs, to spell, or unspell, what held beauty lacks? “To Have Loved” is a poem about the roles men and women sometimes play during times of war. Paris is no longer fully Helen's because he is being called away to battle. The calls of "fame" and "honor" can be stronger than the bonds of love. Helen feels that she is obliged to offer Paris her body and embraces until he lies dead (the "pall and ashes"). But she also feels that she has become an object, like the polished sword he carries, if he can choose it over her. In the final line "held beauty" has multiple meanings. Helen is being held physically by a man she may not see again. She is being held back from going with him because she is "only a woman." She is being held in a tower where everything will change if her husband dies. Will she have to find another man? If so, what will she have to do in order to ensure his protection? The face that famously "launched ten thousand ships" may prove to be her downfall, or it could be her salvation if she plays her cards right. This poem could, in some circumstances, perhaps help a soldier better understand his wife or lover's complex position.

Throughout history, there have been many different gods that have come and gone. Has anyone ever invented a god and then been found out? If so, what was their motive? HUMAN GODS AND GOD-MAKERS by Michael R. Burch There are thousands of “gods” and all of them were invented, from Zeus to Jesus, but in most cases we don’t know the names of the inventors. There are some candidates, however. The first poet we know by name, Enheduanna, elevated her favorite goddess, Inanna, over the pantheon of ancient Sumerian gods. In effect, Enheduanna created the first feminist goddess and she ruled with an iron fingernail! Enheduanna, the daughter of the famous King Sargon the Great of Akkad, is the first ancient writer whose name remains known today. She appears to be the first named poet in human history and the first known author of prayers and hymns. Enheduanna, who lived circa 2285-2250 BCE, is also one of the first women we know by name. Enheduanna revamped her pantheon long before the Yahwist edited the texts of the Hebrew Bible (the Old Testament to Christians) to make his favored god, Yahweh, the supreme god. The Yahwist had his murderous deity replace the more benevolent father-god El (the source of “el” in names like Israel, Michael and Gabriel). First, the Yahwist got rid of Yahweh’s consort, Asherah, in a messy divorce, then his father El, and finally all the other gods completely! It was the Israelite version of Game of Thrones. But the Yahwist was a Johnny-come-lately, as Enheduanna predated him by around 1,700 years! Herodotus, who has been called the “father of history,” said Homer and Hesiod created the ancient Greek gods: It was Hesiod and Homer who first explained to the Greeks the birth of the gods, gave them their names, assigned them their honours and spheres of expertise, and revealed their appearance. So we have four possible early candidates, although in all likelihood someone else created the gods in question and these individuals merely enhanced their reputations (and their own, in the process). Interestingly, Naram-Sin of Akkad, the grandson of King Sargon and thus a relative of Enheduanna, was the first Mesopotamian king known to have claimed divinity for himself, taking the title "God of Akkad." Other human beings who claimed to be gods include Alexander the Great, Yahweh ben Yahweh (Hulon Mitchell, Jr.), and Jesus Christ (if he actually claimed to be god, which I think doubtful). This category would also include Egyptian pharaohs like Ramses I-XI, Roman emperors like Augustus, Chinese emperors beginning with Qin Shi Huang, and Japanese emperors like Hirohito. Imhotep was an ancient Egyptian architect and physician who was elevated to a god two thousand years after his death, becoming the god of medicine and healing. But due to the time gap, we can’t accuse him of deifying himself! Amenhotep was also deified. Romulus and Remus, the legendary founders of Rome, became gods. Many of the alleged “miracles” of Jesus, including dying, being resurrected, appearing to his friends, then ascending into heaven, were performed by Romulus 750 years prior to the purported birth of Jesus. Julius Caesar was defied two years after his death by the Roman senate. All idols with feet of clay, perhaps, but idols nonetheless. by Michael R. Burch

Who is better, Wilt or Magic? Magic Johnson was a great, great player. I have Magic in my all-time top six, but Wilt Chamberlain was far more dominant and is my basketball GOAT. Here’s why… WILT CHAMBERLAIN IS THE NBA GOAT by Michael R. Burch I find it amusing that anyone can propose Michael Jordan, LeBron James, or anyone beside Wilt Chamberlain as the GOAT. I find it amusing that anyone can possibly think MJ, Kobe or LeBron or anyone else is the GOAT. WHAT ABOUT WIN SHARES? What about Win Shares, VORP, PER and other advanced stats? Wilt is third in Win Shares to Kareem and LeBron. But there are three enormous caveats: I believe the third point applies to Win Shares, VORP, PER and other stats that don’t take blocked shots and steals into consideration for players of the past like Wilt. In any case, for me Wilt is the GOAT and no one else is all that close, even with his incomplete stats. WILT CHAMBERLAIN IN THE POSTSEASON One “reason” commonly given for Wilt not being the GOAT is that “he played poorly in the playoffs.” This is a myth, like the earth being flat and tomatoes being poisonous. In reality, these are Wilt’s incredible playoff stats: 1959-60: 33.2 ppg, 25.8 rpg 1960-61: 37.0 ppg, 23.0 rpg 1961-62: 35.0 ppg, 26.6 rpg 1963-64: 34.7 ppg, 25.2 rpg 1964-65: 29.3 ppg, 27.2 rpg 1965-66: 28.0 ppg, 30.2 rpg Wilt obviously dominated in the postseason. For some reason many basketball fans say Wilt “sucked” in the playoffs. Yes, and some “deep thinkers” say the earth is flat… Wilt averaged 30.4 points, 27.0 rebounds and 4.5 assists in 67 playoff games from the 1959-60 to the 1966-67 seasons. Wilt also averaged 8.3 blocks per game in the playoffs. And he hit 51.5% of his field goal attempts despite being banged by multiple defenders. If your team had a player with those stats in the playoffs, you would hail him as a demigod! Due to criticism that he scored too much, Wilt stopped trying to score in the second half of his career and focused on other phases of the game. Still, despite not trying to score for half his career, and struggling with bad knees as he aged, these were Wilt’s career playoff averages: Wilt Chamberlain averaged 24.5 rebounds, 22.5 points and 4.2 assists in 160 games in the playoffs, along with somewhere around 8.3 blocks per game. Let’s consider how “clutch” he was in the biggest games. Wilt dominated in the postseason, just as he did in the regular season, but he was one man and basketball is a team game. Bill Russell and the Celtics had a superteam, and that is why they won 11 rings in 13 seasons. Contrary to popular belief, Bill Russell did not “shut down” the Big Dipper. THE MYTHS OF 1969 I have heard it argued that Wilt “choked” in 1969 when the Lakers lost to the Celtics in the NBA Finals. I have heard it claimed that the Lakers had a “superteam” and that Wilt cannot be the GOAT because he lost with a superteam. But let’s consider facts: First, championships are team accomplishments, not individual accomplishments. The 1969 Celtics had six Hall-of-Famers (Bill Russell, John Havlicek, Sam Jones, Bailey Howell, Don Nelson and Tom “Satch” Sanders). They also had very capable players in Larry Siegfried (14 ppg), Em Bryant (11 ppg), Don Cheney and Jim Barnes. That was a very deep team. There is also a misconception that the Celtics were a lot “older” than the Lakers. But Elgin Baylor and Wilt Chamberlain were 34 and 32, respectively, and both had bad knees. Jerry West was 30 and fatigued. The Celtics got 55.2 points per game in the Finals from their under-30 players, while the Lakers got less than half that, 22.8 ppg, from their under-30 players. Second, the Lakers “big three” was playing together for the first year. The Celtics had been a championship team for a decade. Third, the Lakers only won 55 games, so it was hardly a “super team.” Many NBA teams have had more than 55 wins. Baylor had bad knees and was no longer a superstar. He averaged 18 ppg in the Finals on just .397 shooting from the floor. After the Lakers’ top two players, the Celts were better across the board. West played great despite fatigue and injuries, Wilt outplayed Russell, but the rest of the Celts outplayed the rest of the Lakers. The younger, healthier Havlicek was much better than Baylor at SF, scoring 28.3 points, grabbing 11.0 rebounds and handing out 4.4 assists per game. Fourth, by game three Jerry West was complaining of exhaustion. Then West pulled his hamstring in game five and had to be carried off the court. He was limping in the remaining games and the Lakers only had two point guards on their roster. Fifth, the Lakers had a chance to win game seven but Lakers head coach Butch Van Breda Kolff refused to put Chamberlain back in the game after he’d recovered from a knee injury. Keeping the GOAT out of game seven of the Finals got Dummkopf Kolff fired. Sixth, the Celtics got two very lucky rolls on critical shots in games four and seven. Otherwise, the Lakers might have won either game, and the series. Seventh, it seems silly to say that one series determines who is or isn’t the GOAT. RING BLING In the comments I have been informed that the reason Wilt is not the GOAT is “rings.” But that makes no sense, because championships are team accomplishments. The ring thing is mostly bling, and if rings add zing, Bill Russell’s the king! —Michael R. Burch  If rings determine the GOAT, there is only one possible GOAT: Bill Russell, who won 11 rings in 13 seasons. Michael Jordan and LeBron James are not even in the running. But Bill Russell said himself that Wilt Chamberlain was the GOAT, because Russell knew that his Boston teams were better than Wilt’s teams and that he wasn’t winning championships because he was the better player. Those great Celtics teams sometimes had five Hall-of-Famers starting and two or three more on the bench. The Celtics dynasty had the following 14 Hall-of-Famers… There’s no mystery as to why the Celtics won 11 rings in 13 seasons. They had a superteam with 13 Hall-of-Fame players and perhaps the greatest coach and executive in the history of professional sports. Blaming Wilt Chamberlain for not being able to beat 13 Hall-of-Famers by himself seems both weird and wrong to me. Finally, in regard to counting rings, if rings determine the greatness of individual players… Robert Horry must be seven times greater than Oscar Robertson, Jerry West, Dr. J, Moses Malone, Dirk Nowitzki, Kevin Garnett, Clyde Drexler, Gary Payton, Paul Pierce, Jason Kidd, et al. And Horry must be infinitely better than Elgin Baylor, Charles Barkley, Karl Malone, John Stockton, Chris Paul, Dominique Wilkins, et al. This is why counting rings makes no sense to me, when evaluating individuals. There are great players like Elgin Baylor and Charles Barkley who never won a championship. There are great players like Oscar Robertson, Jerry West and Dr. J who only won one championship. Were they all “losers”? Did they all “choke” repeatedly in the playoffs? Or do teams win championships, not individuals? The question is rhetorical. WILT VS. KAREEM Wilt remained a dominant defensive center even in his mid-thirties with bad knees. For example, the information below was provided by Phillip Schuman in the comments to another answer of mine here on Quora about the 1971-1972 Lakers team: That Lakers team had to beat the defending champs, the Bucks, in the Western Conference finals that year. Kareem, in his third year, was on fire, averaging over 30 field goal attempts per game, and putting up averages of 33.7 points, 17.5 rebounds, and 4.8 assists. (Blocks and steals were still not recorded that year.) The 35-year-old Wilt led all players with his 19.5 rebound average, matched Kareem’s series high 45.8 minutes per game, and forced him into shooting .117 below his season average (.457 vs .574). WILT VS. JORDAN We also need to keep in mind that the NBA changed its rules and the interpretations of its rules to make it easier for Michael Jordan to drive to the basket and wow fans with his dunks, but the NBA changed its rules to make it harder for Goliath to dominate. And yet Wilt led the NBA in field goal percentage nine times, while Jordan never came close to leading in field goal percentage. Nor did LeBron James or Kobe Bryant. THE MYTH OF ELEVATION by Michael R. Burch In the comments it has been claimed that players like Michael Jordan and LeBron James “elevate” the play of their teammates, while Wilt didn’t. But Jordan didn’t elevate his teammates to a championship for his first six years in the NBA. Is Trump a Fascist? by Michael R. Burch As an editor, publisher and translator of Holocaust poetry, I am understandably very concerned about any possible resurgence of fascism in the modern world. But to be honest, I never imagined that it could happen here in the United States. That assurance, however, was shattered when I heard some of the things Donald Trump said during his presidential campaign. Knowing what happened to millions of Jews, Gypsies, Slavs and other “undesirables” during World War II and the Holocaust, I shuddered to think of fascism taking control of the world’s most powerful military, not to mention thousands of nukes. Is it possible that Trump is a fascist, as has been suggested by articles in New Republic, The Nation and other reputable publications? Where there is considerable smoke, may there be fire as well? But how can we tell? Socrates would tell us that before we enter into a debate, we must define our terms. So what, exactly, is fascism? In his essay “Ur-Fascism” (or “Eternal Fascism”), Umberto Eco listed fourteen properties of fascist ideology. Eco said that “it is enough that one of them be present to allow fascism to coagulate around it.” Thus, the presence of just one fascist trait can be very dangerous. Let’s see how many of the fourteen seem to apply to Donald Trump ... (1) “The Cult of Tradition” is characterized by cultural syncretism, even at the risk of internal contradiction. When all truth has already been revealed by Tradition, no new learning can occur, only further interpretation and refinement. Trump is so “traditional” that he equated homosexual marriage with new-fangled golf putters! (Never mind that odd-looking putters and gay marriage do no harm to anyone.) Trump invokes the cult of tradition when he defends discrimination against gay marriage. Trump is popular with evangelical Christians—four out of five evangelicals voted for him according to exit polls—because he embraces the “wisdom” of their received Tradition. (Never mind that the Bible endorses slavery, sex slavery, infanticide, matricide and the stoning to death of children!) Trump demands that everyone accept the tradition of standing during the national anthem. Why? Trump shows no evidence of ever questioning how he “knows” what he “knows.” He just knows, and there is no higher truth. Thus, new learning cannot occur. [Score: Trump 1.0 out of 1.0] (2) “The Rejection of Modernism” views the rationalistic development of Western culture since the Enlightenment as a descent into depravity. Tribal "wisdom" trumps science, pardon the pun. Trump’s evangelical supporters reject homosexual marriage and a woman’s right to choose as “depravity.” They also claim that Islam is a “false” and “depraved” religion, while ignoring the many very similar verses in the Bible and Koran. They insist that climate change is a "hoax," perhaps because their all-powerful "god" who controls nature would never let it happen. Trump ignores the evidence-based findings of American intelligence agencies to go with his "gut." [Score: Trump 2.0 out of 2.0] (3) “The Cult of Action for Action’s Sake” dictates that action is of value in itself, and should be taken without intellectual reflection. This, says Eco, is connected with anti-intellectualism and irrationalism, and often manifests in attacks on modern culture and science. Trump’s mindless attacks on the EPA, the Climate Action Plan, the Paris Accords, NATO and the EU are cases in point. While often not seeming to have any sort of developed plan, Trump loves to be seen as a man of action, charging forth, even when he appears to be tilting at windmills (as with the Trump Shutdown over his imaginary border "wall"). Trump's "Muslim ban" is another example: "In a broad sense this reflects the cult of action for action’s sake, especially insofar as the pretense that summary discrimination against and persecution of Muslims writ large for the actions of terrorists amounts to 'doing something.'" [Score: Trump 3.0 out of 3.0] (4) “Disagreement Is Treason” devalues intellectual discourse and critical reasoning as barriers to action, out of fear that such analysis will expose the contradictions embodied in a syncretistic faith. “In modern culture,” says Eco, “the scientific community praises disagreement as a way to improve knowledge. For Ur-Fascism, disagreement is treason.” Trump did not allow peaceful protests at his political rallies and said that he longed for the days when protesters ended up in the hospital, going as far as to say that he would like to punch protesters himself. He joined in chants of “lock her up” after Hillary Clinton confronted him with intellectual and fact-based arguments that exposed the errors and contradictions in his theories and plans. As president, Trump has fired all the "adults in the room" in order to surround himself with yes-men and yes-women. [Score: Trump 4.0 out of 4.0] (5) “Fear of Difference” is used to stir up racist sentiments against foreigners and immigrants. Trump shot to the top of the polls when in his first campaign speech he portrayed illegal immigrants as being “rapists” and “drug pushers” with only very limited exceptions. Of course that was far from the truth, since illegal immigrants commit fewer crimes, on a percentage basis, than the general population. Muslims of all stripes are another Trump target because they are all seen as potential terrorists: "Trump renders himself cause and cure of the problem of terrorism through binary Othering of the terrorist peril, an approach that also appeals to popular fear of difference." This fear of the Other led to Trump's infamous "Muslim ban." [Score: Trump 5.0 out of 5.0] (6) “Appeal to a Frustrated Middle Class” who fear economic pressure from the demands and aspirations of lower social groups. "Ur-Fascism derives from individual or social frustration. That is why one of the most typical features of the historical fascism was the appeal to a frustrated middle class, a class suffering from an economic crisis or feelings of political humiliation, and frightened by the pressure of lower social groups." One may postulate that this is how Trump won the presidential election: by focusing on Rust Belt “swing” states where the white middle-class had lost jobs and their employment prospects were less than optimal. These Hallowed Halls by Michael R. Burch a young Romantic Poet mourns the passing of an age . . . I. A final stereo fades into silence and now there is seldom a murmur to trouble the slumber of these ancient halls. I stand by a window where others have watched the passage of time—alone, not untouched. And I am as they were . . . unsure . . . for the days stretch out ahead, a bewildering maze. II. Ah, faithless lover— that I had never touched your breast, nor felt the stirrings of my heart, which until that moment had peacefully slept. For now I have known the exhilaration of a heart that has vaulted the Pinnacle of Love, and the result of each such infatuation— the long freefall to earth, as the moon glides above. III. A solitary clock chimes the hour from far above the campus, but my peers, returning from their dances, heed it not. And so it is that we fail to gauge Time’s speed because He moves so unobtrusively about His task. Still, when at last we reckon His mark upon our lives, we may well be surprised at His thoroughness. IV. Ungentle maiden— when Time has etched His little lines so carelessly across your brow, perhaps I will love you less than now. And when cruel Time has stolen your youth, as He certainly shall in course, perhaps you will wish you had taken me along with my broken heart, even as He will take you with yours. V. A measureless rhythm rules the night— few have heard it, but I have shared it, and its secret is mine. To put it into words is as to extract the sweetness from honey and must be done as gently as a butterfly cleans its wings. But when it is captured, it is gone again; its usefulness is only that it lulls to sleep. VI. So sleep, my love, to the cadence of night, to the moans of the moonlit hills' bass chorus of frogs, while the deep valleys fill with the nightjar’s shrill, cryptic trills. But I will not sleep this night, nor any . . . how can I—when my dreams are always of your perfect face ringed by soft whorls of fretted lace, framed by your perfect pillowcase? VII. If I had been born when knights roamed the earth and mad kings ruled savage lands, I might have turned to the ministry, to the solitude of a monastery. But there are no monks or hermits today— theirs is a lost occupation carried on, if at all, merely for sake of tradition. For today man abhors solitude— he craves companions, song and drink, seldom seeking a quiet moment, to sit alone, by himself, to think. VIII. And so I cannot shut myself off from the rest of the world, to spend my days in philosophy and my nights in tears of self-sympathy. No, I must continue as best I can, and learn to keep my thoughts away from those glorious, uproarious moments of youth, centuries past though lost but a day. IX. Yes, I must discipline myself and adjust to these lackluster days when men display no chivalry and romance is the "old-fashioned" way. X. A single stereo flares into song and the first faint light of morning has pierced the sky's black awning once again. XI. This is a sacred place, for those who leave, leave better than they came. But those who stay, while they are here, add, with their sleepless nights and tears, quaint sprigs of ivy to the walls of these hallowed halls. I vividly remember writing the first version of “These Hallowed Halls” early my freshman year of college as I watched my peers returning from rush week parties by the light of an eerie moon.

Burch I think we have to rank Iron Mike Tyson on his overall record, but we can also consider where he ranked at his peak. I will give both evaluations after a brief recap of his career. Feb. 10, 1990: 37-0, age 23, Top 3-5 Up to his Feb. 11, 1990 upset loss to the massive underdog James “Buster” Douglas, it seemed Mike Tyson, who was 37-0 and had seldom really been tested, was well on his way to becoming a top five heavyweight of all time. Perhaps even top three with Muhammad Ali and Joe Louis. After all, only four boxers had gone ten rounds with Tyson, and all four of those fights were unanimous decisions in his favor. However, even before his first loss the cracks were beginning to show. In 1988, after Tyson had knocked out Larry Holmes in the fourth round, then Michael Spinks in just 91 seconds, he seemed to be on top of the boxing world. However, Tyson had separated from his wife Robin Givens with rumors of physical abuse, he had crashed his car into a tree and the incident had been reported as a potential suicide attempt by some newspapers. Tyson fired his longtime trainer Kevin Rooney. At some point Tyson began partying 24/7, even when training for fights. He became a cocaine and sex addict. Don King was seen as taking advantage of him. And how good was Tyson’s competition really? He had defeated a 39-year-old Larry Holmes who had come out of retirement after losing twice to the smaller Michael Spinks. Many boxing experts and fans considered Spinks to be undersized and underpowered for a heavyweight. It wasn’t exactly the Golden Age of Heavyweights that Tyson had been dominating. Feb. 10, 1990: 37-1, age 23, Top 5-10 After his stunning upset loss to Buster Douglas, additional doubts had been raised, but Tyson was still just 23 years old, upsets do happen in boxing, and Tyson went on to win his next four fights, including two victories over Donovan “Razor” Ruddock that left Tyson 41-1 just two days short of his 25th birthday. June 28, 1991: 41-1, age 25, Top 5-8 But in 1992, Tyson was convicted of rape and sentenced to six years in prison. He was released on parole after three years. Tyson went on to win his next four fights, leaving him 45-1 at age 30. None of those fights went past the third round. However, Tyson had stopped using the “peek-a-boo” technique that had made him great to become a headhunter in search of quick wins. This made him susceptible to boxers he couldn’t knock out, such as Evander Holyfield and Lennox Lewis. Sept. 7, 1995: 45-1, age 30, Top 5-7 At that point in his career, Tyson still had a chance to be a top five heavyweight, but he proceeded to go off the rails, losing twice to Evander Holyfield and biting off part of Holyfield’s ear in the rematch. In his last seven fights Tyson was an unimpressive 3-2-2. At age 35, Tyson won one fight against Brian Nielsen, then was knocked out by Lennox Lewis, leaving the aging Tyson 49-4-2, with fading hopes for the top ten, much less the top five. Tyson would lose two of his last three fights, leaving him 50-6-2 at age 38. Why in Major League Baseball does a scuffed up baseball make a difference? NOTORIOUS SPITBALLERS AND SCUFFERS by Michael R. Burch Baseballs obey the laws of physics and a scuffed baseball results in more wind resistance. Since the scuffing is not uniform, increased wind resistance here and there will result in a thrown baseball’s arc through the air becoming more erratic and thus less predictable. And ultimately, harder to hit. Who were the most famous spitballers and scuffers? (Unhappy hitters might prefer the term “infamous.”) Famous and infamous spitballers and scuffers include hall-of-famers Whitey Ford, Gaylord Perry and Don Sutton. Don Sutton’s nickname was "Black & Decker" due to the lengths he went to mutilate horsehide. Lengths that included cutting, scuffing, sandpapering, and otherwise disfiguring innocent baseballs. Legend has it that when Sutton met notorious greaseballer Gaylord Perry for the first time, Perry handed him a tube of Vaseline, and Sutton returned the favor by handing Perry a sheet of sandpaper. Famous scuffers include hall-of-famer Whitey Ford, who even used his wedding ring to mutilitate baseballs before throwing them! In an interview with Hal McCoy, Ford admitting using his belt buckle, catcher Elston Howard's shinguard, and even his wedding ring to scuff the ball. Is nothing sacred to scuffers? Ford also admitted using "gunk" composed of baby oil, turpentine and resin. Spitballers like Gaylord Perry have preferred vaseline and various other “ointments” to alter the trajectories of their pitches. According to Peter Gammons in a 1989 Sports Illustrated article: Perry has admitted to having used K-Y jelly, vaseline, saliva, fishing-line wax, resin, sweat and dirt to make baseballs do peculiar things. However, he may not have been as much of an outlaw as he led us to believe. Dave Duncan, who was Perry's catcher with the Cleveland Indians in 1974, a season in which Perry went 21-13, claims Perry threw only one spitter that year. "He had a great sinker and just kept up the act [his fidgeting on the mound] to make hitters believe he was loading up the ball." says Duncan. "So they focused on trying to catch him cheating instead of concentrating on how he was pitching them." Though opponents watched him closely. Perry was caught throwing an illegal pitch only once in his career. Preacher Roe admitted employing a "Beech-Nut slider" less than a year after retiring, in a 1955 Sports Illustrated article by Dick Young: "One way I figured out to keep my fingers clean, was to wipe ‘em on the visor of my baseball cap. It looked like I was adjusting it on my head. I always made certain the visor was kept clean. I even went to the trouble of brushing it off with a towel on the bench between innings. "It didn’t take long for some of the hitters to figure there was something going on between my spitter and the way I fingered the cap. That was just fine for me. I started using the gesture as a decoy. That was as good as the pitch itself. From then on, even when I wasn’t going to throw a wet one, I’d go to my cap just to cross them up." Art Fowler threw a spitball during his major league career (1954-1964), but is more famous as Billy Martin's longtime pitching coach. Fowler taught the tricks of the spitball trade to Oakland A's pitchers Mike Norris, Rick Langford, Steve McCatty, Matt Keough and Brian Kingman.
